title: GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix
content:
Computer Science > Information Retrieval

    Title:GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping recommender systems by enabling richer modeling of users, content, and context directly in natural language. At Netflix, we are exploring this direction through GenRec, an LLM-backed recommendation ranker built on top of an in-house foundational LLM. GenRec follows a two-phase framework: Phase 1 adapts an open-source LLM to Netflix data, developing deep understanding of the catalog and member behavior while balancing capabilities such as content understanding and instruction following. Phase 2 post-trains this foundation model with recommendation-ranking specific data, labels, and reward signals, aiming to align the ranker with business requirements and long-term member satisfaction.
This paper focuses on Phase 2 and the transition from a traditional discriminative ranker with thousands of engineered features to an LLM-backed ranker driven by verbalized user histories and context. We describe our design for input verbalization and context engineering, post-training data construction, reward integration, model architecture, and a cost-constrained serving design based on a prefill-only inference approach. We report results from a large-scale A/B test comparing GenRec against the current production ranker model, where we show that a GenRec model trained with substantially fewer Phase-2 labeled training examples and input signals can achieve statistically significant gains in offline and online metrics. We discuss how LLM-backed recommenders could shift the recommendation paradigm: from feature engineering to context engineering, and from bespoke architectures to shared foundation backbones. We also outline practical lessons for serving such systems under real-world resource constraints.

report.summary: Netflix's GenRec replaces traditional recommendation rankers with an LLM, using context engineering and fewer training examples to beat production metrics.
report.background: Recommendation systems have long relied on discriminative models with thousands of manually engineered features, which are costly to maintain and limited in capturing user intent. Netflix built GenRec on an in-house foundational LLM to shift that paradigm. The two-phase approach starts with adapting an open-source LLM to Netflix catalog and member behavior, then post-trains it specifically for ranking using labels and reward signals. This paper focuses on the second phase, detailing input verbalization, context engineering, post-training data construction, and a prefill-only serving design for cost efficiency. A large-scale A/B test showed GenRec achieved statistically significant offline and online gains despite using substantially fewer labeled examples and input signals than the production ranker, signaling a broader move from feature engineering to context engineering.
key_points: GenRec uses a two-phase training strategy: first, an LLM is adapted to understand Netflix's catalog and member behavior; second, it is post-trained with ranking-specific data and reward signals to align with business goals and member satisfaction.

The paper describes a clear shift from traditional feature engineering to context engineering. Instead of thousands of handcrafted features, systems rely on verbalized user histories and contextual prompts to make recommendations.

A cost-constrained serving design based on prefill-only inference makes LLM-backed ranking feasible under real-world infrastructure limits, addressing one of the biggest barriers to production deployment.

In a large-scale A/B test, GenRec outperformed the current production ranker on both offline and online metrics, despite being trained with substantially fewer Phase-2 labeled examples and input signals.
The findings point toward a future of shared foundation backbones for recommender systems, reducing bespoke model architectures and enabling faster adaptation across use cases.
report.impact: For the AI industry, GenRec offers evidence that LLM-backed rankers can perform well in large-scale production systems, likely accelerating similar efforts at other platforms. Developers will need to build skills in prompt and context engineering, post-training pipelines, and cost-aware serving rather than traditional feature engineering. For regular users, this could mean more relevant, context-sensitive recommendations and improved long-term satisfaction. However, the approach raises practical concerns around compute cost, latency, and reliance on foundation model providers; the prefill-only serving trick shows optimization can mitigate these, but it may not fully eliminate the resource gap for smaller companies.
report.tools: Netflix has not open-sourced GenRec, but readers can explore related open-source ecosystems: Hugging Face Transformers for fine-tuning LLMs, TRL for DPO/RLHF post-training, vLLM for optimized inference and prefill strategies, and LangChain for context/prompt engineering. Open foundation models like Llama and Mistral are good starting points for building LLM-backed recommender prototypes.
